title: TitanMPAS - a new global and regional Titan atmospheric circulation model. Part I: Global model results
comment: Submitted to The Planetary Science Journal
summary: We developed TitanMPAS, a new Titan global and regional climate model, to simulate atmospheric dynamics and methane cycles. It integrates the non-hydrostatic MPAS dynamical core and TitanWRF physics parameterizations, with corrections to relax the thin-atmosphere assumptions on the gravity and curvature terms. TitanMPAS improves upon TitanWRF by incorporating a better moist convection parameterization and the observed surface properties. Long-term simulations ($>$100 Titan years) with a high resolution of $1^\circ$ and the realistic topography show that TitanMPAS is able to produce the stratospheric superrotation with typical equatorial wind speed over $\rm 120\,ms^{-1}$ and the maximum zonal wind speed exceeding $\rm 170\,ms^{-1}$ . Besides the good match of temperature profiles to the Cassini CIRS observations, the simulated wind, temperature and methane abundance in the troposphere match well with Huygens probe in-situ measurements. TitanMPAS also captures the major features of seasonal methane precipitation distribution patterns inferred from the observed cloud activities, as well as the vertical and latitudinal variations of methane abundance in the reanalysis of Cassini VIMS data. Resolution sensitivity studies show that higher resolution produces faster stratospheric superrotation, as well as stronger near-surface wind due to better resolved terrain variations. We further demonstrate that, despite the weak solar insolation, the near-surface temperature, pressure, wind magnitude and methane abundance all exhibit diurnal variations. Lastly, we show potential impacts of topography on methane transport and eddy momentum flux in both troposphere and stratosphere, which should be investigated in a future study.

title: Coherent radio emission at 45 MHz from the nearby planet-hosting star GJ 725A
summary: Ultra-low-frequency (<100 MHz) coherent radio emission from exoplanet-hosting stellar systems carries information about planetary and stellar magnetic fields, as well as the space weather environment - information that is difficult to obtain at other wavelengths. We carried out the circularly polarized LOFAR LBA Sky Survey, the most sensitive circularly polarized survey in this frequency range, using the LOFAR low-band antenna system. As part of this untargeted search, we detected a signal in a 1h observation that is coincident with the quiescent, planet-hosting, solar-neighborhood M dwarf GJ 725A at a distance of 3.5 pc. The signal has a high circular polarization fraction of $74\pm16$% and a peak brightness of $B=135\pm17$ mJy/beam between 42 MHz and 50 MHz. It was undetected in the 50-66 MHz range, with a 3$σ$ upper limit of $B<48$ mJy/beam, corresponding to a drop of at least a factor 3 across 12 MHz, and indicating a strong spectral feature or cutoff around 50 MHz. Our detection represents the lowest-frequency confirmed detection of a stellar system. Based on the high estimated brightness temperature ($\sim10^{14}$ K), transient character and polarization fraction, the emission is most plausibly attributed to the electron cyclotron maser instability. The available observations are not sufficient to identify the astrophysical origin of the emission. We consider three plausible scenarios: auroral emission of a yet undetected wide-orbit giant planet with a magnetic field $B\geq18$ G, star-planet interaction with the known 11 d orbit terrestrial planet GJ 725Ab, or an origin due to stellar magnetic activity. Ultra-low-frequency monitoring, combined with new, preferably simultaneous observations in the X-rays, UV, and H$α$, and a search for a wide-orbit (thousands of days) giant planet across the full allowed parameter space will allow us to distinguish between these scenarios.

title: Estimations for strong and weak hot Jupiter magnetism: A Python package with interpolators and scaling laws
comment: 21 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics. Under review
summary: Hot Jupiters (HJs) are commonly thought to host the strongest dynamo-generated magnetic fields among exoplanets, exceeding Jupiter's by up to an order of magnitude, which can potentially induce observable star-planet interaction (SPI) and planetary radio emission. However, while several indirect, model-dependent estimates of HJ magnetic fields have been reported from SPIs and recent transmission spectroscopy diagnostics, no unambiguous direct (radio) detection has yet been achieved. We aim to provide a range of magnetic field estimates for HJs, considering the mechanisms responsible for inflation and the convective flux entering the magnetic field scaling law. Given that their dynamos operate in the fast-rotating regime (Rossby number <~ 0.1), we combine one-dimensional evolutionary interior models with magnetic field scaling laws under two limiting heating scenarios: deep and shallow energy depositions. The deep-heating scenario maximizes convective heat flux in the dynamo and predicts strong magnetic fields of up to ~100 G, whereas shallow heating, which is arguably more realistic for most proposed physical mechanisms, weakens convection and yields much weaker fields of O(1) G. The strong field scenario is compatible with SPI indirect detections, and the weak field scenario is in agreement with recent atmospheric constraints. We derive scaling law relations based on observables (planetary mass, radius, and/or incident stellar flux): Bstrong = 19 M_P^0.6 R_P^1.7 G; Bweak = 0.8 M_P^1.5 R_P^-1.2 G. These predictions provide a framework for interpreting future atmospheric wind measurements, SPI signatures, and radio observations, which may ultimately discriminate between competing interior-heating scenarios.

title: New optimisations for exact, scalable 2D Gaussian process inference, with applications to astronomical time-series
summary:
Astronomical datasets often consist of a grid of datapoints in two or more dimensions, such as images, spectroscopic time-series, and imaging time-series. Gaussian processes (GPs) are a powerful tool for dealing with correlated noise in these data, arising from both astrophysical and instrumental systematics. Despite this, popular GP optimisations such as celerite are largely restricted to 1D datasets. Extensions to 2D data typically come with limited flexibility or poor scaling. As a motivating example, this limitation is significant for transiting exoplanet spectroscopy with JWST, as current analyses typically assume each spectroscopic light curve is statistically independent, despite many potential sources of wavelength-correlation, including detector readout noise and stellar granulation. This introduces a potential bias in atmospheric retrievals which is typically ignored.
  To solve this problem, we present new, exact GP optimisations implemented in the JAX-based package luas, which extend 1D GP optimisations to multidimensional data using Kronecker product algebra. These GP optimisations are highly flexible, permit efficient analysis of 2D datasets containing millions of datapoints, and in many cases have a cheaper cost than transit light curve modelling. These optimisations are key to pushing the limits of exoplanet spectroscopy to smaller targets around bright host stars, as we increasingly hit instrumental and astrophysical noise floors. We suggest further applications to the analysis of ground-based high resolution spectroscopic time-series, extreme precision radial velocities, and high-contrast imaging, drawing on the connection that certain 2D GP models represent a probabilistic generalisation of PCA. Applications may even extend to machine learning and geostatistics, as we present novel optimisations for the Linear Mixing Model and the Linear Model of Coregionalisation.

title: CO gaps in cold transition disks around low-mass stars
summary: Transition disks with large inner dust cavities are promising targets to study planet formation, as these disks are likely hosting massive planetary companions. The structure of gas and dust inside the cavity are crucial for understanding the potential of planet formation in the regions. We investigate the structure of gas and dust in a sample of three cold, inclined transition disks around K and M stars without evidence for an inner dusty disk. We present new high-resolution ALMA Band 6 data of both 230 GHz continuum at 0.02" (~3 au) resolution and the 12CO 2-1, 13CO 2-1, C18O 2-1 isotopologues at 0.12" (~20 au) resolution. We analyze the radial profiles, compute the brightness temperatures, and derive estimates of the gas and dust content of the inner disk at 1 au. All three disks show dust cavities of 30-40 au in radius. The CO emission extends inside the cavity with progressively smaller CO cavity radii for the more abundant isotopologues. The 13CO brightness temperature profile is similar to that of other transition disks and full disks. No inner dust disk is detected in the ALMA continuum, consistent with the lack of near-infrared excess. Considering the accretion rates, the gas-to-dust ratio in the inner disk at 1 au is estimated to be as high as 10^5. No significant differences in the brightness temperature or in the gas-to-dust ratio are found between our disks and other transition disks around more luminous stars, contrary to expectations. This highlights the importance of individual-target studies through thermochemical modeling or multi-transition analyses to constrain the dust and gas structures in the cavity. The observed disk structures could be explained by super-Jovian companion on eccentric orbits, but further modeling is needed to confirm this conclusion.

title: Validation of Habitable Zone Limits with a New Radiative-Convective Equilibrium Climate Model
comment: This paper is dedicated to Jim Kasting
summary: The habitable zone (HZ) boundaries calculated with the Clima one-dimensional radiative-convective equilibrium (RCE) model have served as a standard reference for exoplanet target selection for three decades, but they have never been independently validated with a comparable model. We present ExoColumn, a new one-dimensional RCE model that couples an independently developed atmospheric column physics package to the ExoRT correlated-k radiative transfer core that is also used by the three-dimensional ExoCAM model. We calibrate ExoColumn to present-day conditions, which matches other RCE models to within a few kelvin through the troposphere. Line-by-line benchmarks show that the ExoRT and Clima radiation cores each reproduce the outgoing longwave flux to within a few percent, with the differences due to the spectral line databases used by each model. We follow the same inverse climate modeling method as previous studies have done to find inner edge moist- and runaway-greenhouse limits of 0.970 au and 0.966 au, and an outer-edge maximum-greenhouse limit of 1.611 au at a CO$_2$ partial pressure of 8.7 bar. We extend these calculations to 12 host stars spanning 2000-7200 K and to planets of 0.1, 1, and 5 Earth mass, and we provide updated HZ boundary coefficients for community use. The ExoColumn limits systematically fall closer to the host star than those of Clima but agree to within a few percent in orbital distance, which validates the robustness of the published Clima HZ boundaries.

title: Advances in High-Precision Astrometry for Exoplanet Detection for Astrometric Missions
summary: High-precision astrometry is a cornerstone for detecting Earth-like exoplanets in the habitable zones of nearby solar-type stars and probing the nature of dark matter in galactic environments. Achieving sub-microarcsecond accuracy requires unprecedented control over detector morphology, optical distortion, and astrometric measurement techniques. This paper reviews recent progress in characterizing large format detector at the micropixel scale level, calibrating optical distortion using reference stars, and refining differential astrometry methods to detect the faint astrometric signatures of Earth-mass exoplanets. We highlight the latest developments in the RETINA project, which aims to advance the TRL of GIGAPYX 220 MP CMOS detectors from Pyxalis which are critical components for future space missions such as ESA's Theia and NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO). The project focuses on precise calibration methods, including Young's fringe projection, to monitor pixel geometry and intra-pixel response across gigapixel-scale focal planes. By integrating these advancements, RETINA seeks to enable astrometric detection of Earth-mass exoplanets with a precision of few tens of micropixels on the focal plane. We discuss the technical strategies, laboratory validations, and system-level integration required to achieve these goals, emphasizing the synergy between detector technology, optical calibration, and mission design. These innovations pave the way for next-generation astrometric instruments capable of transforming our understanding of exoplanetary systems and dark matter dynamics.

title: VLT and Keck recovery and characterisation of 2025 SC$_{79}$: linking 'Ayló'chaxnim and Atira asteroids
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables, including appendices. Submitted to A&A
summary: Asteroids near the boundary between the Atira and 'Ayló'chaxnim classes can trace dynamical links between the two populations, but their small solar elongations make recovery and physical characterisation difficult. We recover 2025 SC$_{79}$, measure its optical colours, and investigate its likely source region and transitions between these populations. We combine Keck/LRIS astrometry and VLT/FORS2 four-filter photometry with Bus-DeMeo taxonomic comparisons, published source-model probabilities, and integrations of 10,000 clones drawn from the covariance of JPL solution #2 and followed for 5 Myr in each direction. The SDSS-equivalent colours are $g-r=0.8254_{-0.1339}^{+0.2136}$, $r-i=0.1764_{-0.0540}^{+0.0523}$ and $i-z=-0.4975_{-0.1162}^{+0.1055}$ mag. The V-type class mean gives the closest colour match. At the V-type median albedo $p_V=0.362$, $H=18.83\pm0.15$ mag implies a diameter of $0.379^{+0.027}_{-0.025}$ km. The source model assigns a combined probability of 95.4% to delivery channels associated with the inner Main Belt. The ensemble-mean 'Ayló'chaxnim/Atira residence fractions are 30.2%/69.8% over the preceding 100 kyr and 3.6%/96.0% over the following 100 kyr; the remaining 0.4% of future ensemble time follows collision removal. Clones spend an average of 231 kyr in the 'Ayló'chaxnim class over the preceding 500 kyr and 120 kyr over the following 500 kyr. In the 5-Myr forward integrations, 14.56% of clones collide with Venus, 3.77% with Mercury and 0.22% with Earth. The V-like colours and source-model probabilities favour an origin in the inner Main Belt for 2025 SC$_{79}$. Its clones move between the 'Ayló'chaxnim and Atira populations.
